catalog_locator: Section 'Phonemes of Mkaa’' > 'Vowel phonemes' > 'The reduced vowel', printed p.12 = PDF p.16 (page image rendered and read); supporting statement 'Phonemes of Mkaa’', printed p.1 = PDF p.5; tone printed p.14 = PDF p.18. File: the copy we hold.
catalog_quote: The case of /ə/ deserves particular attention as it appears to not be a full phoneme but rather a reduced vowel allophone conditioned by the stress patterns of Mkaa’. Observe that it never occurs in the prosodically strong stem initial syllable, nor in a closed syllable, nor as a long vowel. Following the glottal stop, a particularly weak consonant, it fully assimilates to V1. Moreover, stress in Mkaa’ appears not to be contrastive, but predictable. Simply put, initial word stress falls on the first stem syllable and then on every other stress unit (mora) to the right. Regular CV syllables are considered to have one mora, long vowels syllables and closed syllables count as having two moras. The actual stress rules are fairly complicated and must take into account the syllable types making up the word.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable: primary stress falls on the stem-initial (root-initial) syllable, which need not be word-initial because nouns and verbs carry inflectional prefixes; prefix syllables and the syllables adjacent to the stem-initial one are unstressed and host reduced/lenis allophones (the reduced vowel [ə] never occurs in the stem-initial syllable). Mkaa' is also a two-tone language (H, L, with downstep), tone being the contrastive suprasegmental.
new_statements.secondary_stress: After the stem-initial stress, stress recurs on every other mora to the right (CV = 1 mora; long-vowel and closed syllables = 2 moras); author notes the detailed rules are 'fairly complicated' and depend on syllable types.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; author hedges ('appears not to be contrastive', 'actual stress rules are fairly complicated'). p.1 adds: 'The stem initial position is not necessarily word initial since verbs and nouns are often preceded by inflectional prefixes. Syllables in non-stem initial position, particularly those adjacent to the stem initial syllable, tend to be unstressed.' Consonant+glide onsets occur only stem-initially, i.e. only in stressed syllables (pp.12-13).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prosodic word = prefixes + stem); statements based on lexicon citation forms (Ewane Etame 1995 lexicon + Shoebox database and author's fieldwork 1996-98 in Bakaka canton, consultant from Ebone village). Tone (H/L) is the distinctive suprasegmental; stress is described as allophone-conditioning prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Spielmann 1998/2003 describes Mkaa' (Bakaka canton near Nkongsamba, Nlonako subdivision; principal consultant from Ebone village), 'the central dialect of the East-Central Group of the Manenguba languages' = Glottolog baka1273 / ISO bqz exactly. Note Glottolog 5.1 sources.bib mis-assigns this Spielmann item to Makaa [mcp] by a computerized match on 'mkaa'; it belongs to bqz. Hedinger 1984's remark is group-level (Proto-Manenguba and all 14 varieties, MKA among them), not Mkaa'-specific.

sources.note: p.1: stem-initial position is prosodically strong; non-stem-initial syllables, esp. those adjacent to the stem-initial syllable, tend to be unstressed and host reduced/lenis allophones. p.12: stress appears non-contrastive and predictable: initial word stress on the first stem syllable, then on every other mora to the right (CV = 1 mora; long-vowel and closed syllables = 2); reduced vowel [ə] never in the stem-initial syllable; C+glide onsets only stem-initial i.e. only in stressed syllables (p.12-13). p.14: two phonemic tones H, L, downstep.

sources.note: Comparative-historical (14 varieties incl. MKA = Mkaa'/Bakaka). Single hedged group-level remark, sec. 5.6 p.223: loss of second root vowels 'could possibly have to do with stress on the stem initial syllable. However, since tone is the main suprasegmental phenomenon which has distinctive function, stress is not often discussed and therefore the relationship of tone and stress is not well understood.' No Mkaa'-specific prosody statement; MKA consonant/vowel systems only (3.2.4.4).
